OBITUARY REFERENCES 
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to 
the passing away of His Majesty King Fahd Bin Abdul Aziz Al Saud, King of 
Saudi Arabia. In the passing away of His Majesty King Fahd, the Kingdom of 
Saudi Arabia has lost a leader and the world an elder statesman. The 
achievements of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia under his leadership stand 
testimony to his vision. 
India has maintained close and friendly relations with Saudi Arabia under 
the leadership of King Fa hd. These bonds have been especially strengthened 
by the presence of the large expatria te Indian community which has found a 
home in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. 
This House joins the ruling family of Saudi Arabia, the leaderhip and the people 
of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in mourning the irreparable loss in the death of 
King Fahd. 
I also refer with profound sorrow to the passing away of Shri Natha Singh, 
a former Member of this House on the 16th July, 2005 at the age of 77 years. 
Shri Natha Singh was born at Lal Basti, Bayana, in the Bharatpur District 
of Rajasthan, in August, 1928. He participated in the freedom movement and 
was imprisoned in 1945. 
A cultivator and a farmer, Shri Singh took keen interest in social reforms 
and uplift of backward classes. He was also associated with various welfare 
organisations. He was President of the Rajasthan Van Shramik Sahakari 
Sangh from 1971 to 1976. 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2005] 
Shri Natha Singh was a Member of the Rajasthan Legislative Assembly from 
1972 to 1977. He represented the State of Rajasthan in this House from April, 
1982 to April, 1988. 
In the passing away of Shri Natha Singh, the country has lost a noted social 
worker. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of His Majesty King Fahd Bin Abdul 
Aziz Al Saud and Shri Natha Singh. 
I request the Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of 
respect to the memory of the departed. 
(The Members then stood in silence for one minute) 
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Secretar y-General will convey to the 
members of the bereaved families our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy.

Utilisation of Rupsi Airport 
*121. SHRI DWIJENDRA NATH SHARMAH: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any proposal to utilise the Rupsi Airport near 
Dhubri in Assam; 
(b) if so, what steps have been taken by Government till now; and 
(c) whether there is any commitment from Government to the NER MPs in 
this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) The possibility of renovation and reconstruction of Rupsi Airport near 
Dhubri in Assam was examined. Inspection of the existing airstrip by Airports 
Authority of India (AAI) at Rupsi near Dhubri in Assam has indicated an estimated 
expenditure of Rs. 65 crores to make it operational. No firm commitment from 
airlines for scheduled operations from Rupsi has been received. Therefore, AAI 
has no proposal to renovate the Rupsi Airport at present.

Investment of pension funds in capital market 
123. SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any proposal for investment of pension fund of Central 
Government employees in the capital market; 
(b) if so, the details thereof including the present status of the above 
proposal; 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2005] 
(c) whether there is any proposal to  allow Foreign Direct Investment 
and Private Fund Managers in the pension fund of Central Government 
employees; and 
(d) if so, the details and the present status of above proposal? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is placed on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) It is envisaged that, unde r the New Pension System, subscribers 
will have a choice of multiple investment options such as options A, B and C. 
Under option A there would be predominant investment in fixed income 
instruments and some investment in equity. Option B would imply greater 
investment in equity. Option C would imply almost equal investment in fixed 
income and equity. Investment guidelines would be framed by the regulator 
through regulations under the proposed Pension Fund Regulatory and 
Development Authority (PFRDA) Bill, 2005. The Standing Committee on 
Finance, which presented its report on the PFRDA Bill on 26th July 2005, have 
recommended, making available to the subscribers, an option of 100% 
investment of pension funds in Government securities. Government had earlier 
indicated to the Standing Committee that an option for investing wholly in debt 
instruments would be considered favourably by the Government. The other 
recommendations of the report of the Committee are also being examined in the 
Ministry of Finance. 
(c) and (d) It is proposed to open up pension funds to competing opera-tors, 
including public sector fund managers and some private sector fund managers. All 
such pension funds would be registered with and regulated by the Pension Fund 
Regulatory and Development Authourity. No decision has yet been taken 
regarding foreign equity participation in the pension sector. The recommendation 
of the Standing Committee on Finance on these issues are being examined.

pipeline the three which probably matter the maximum to India are Myanmar- 
Bangladesh-India and Turkmenistan pipelines to India. I believe both these 
pipelines for different reasons are almost traped in the pipeline.The Myanmar- 
Bangladesh-India pipeline, which probably has the potential for India is stuck with 
the way Bangladesh is bargaining. Turkmenistan, apparently, my limited 
knowledge tells me, has promised more than it produces to preferably European 
market. So we come to the one which still is feasible, that is, the 2,600 
kilometre Iran-Pakistan- India pipeline. I have learnt that it is scheduled to cost 
us $ four billions just for the piping. Mas the Minister worked out as to what 
would be the well-head cost from the point of view of Iran and what would be the 
end cost to the consumers, primarily, the power sector and the fertilizers 
sector? How much would we be paying for transport and transit to Pakistan? 
What would be the end cost? Would it be economically viable? 
SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Sir, I am afraid the request for a brief 
answer is not possible to a complicated question. As regards the pipeline from 
Myanmar, with respect to the substance of what needs to be done between us, 
Myanmar and Bangladesh, there is complete agreement as expressed in the draft 
Memorandum of Understanding that was prepared by the Technical and 
commercial Working Group in February this year. However, there is one non-
operative preambular paragraph in the Draft MoLI which is causing some 
concern. I am glad to inform the House that the hon. Minister of External Affairs 
is scheduled to make a visit to Dhaka in the immediate future, that is, on 6th of 
August. One of my Officers will be accompanying him. We hope that he will be 
able to unite this somewhat knotty problem which has held matters up for the last 
several months. As regards the pipelines from Turkmenistan, it is a fact that 
Pakistan has refused to attend any further meetings of the Steering Committee of 
TAP, unless and until the Turkmenistan Government is able to provide figures of 
certified reserves. That has not yet happened. One of the possible reasons for their 
not providing the certified reserves could be shortage of available gas in that 
country. It is anticipating this that when Pakistanis asked me 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2005] 
to convert TAP which stands for Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan into TAPt, 
by adding India, I suggested that pe rhaps the answer to the fundamental 
problem of availabilities in Turkmenistan might lie in linking this further 
upstream to Uzbekistan which would make it UPTAPI, to Kazakhistan, which 
would make it KUTAPI, to Azerbaijan, which would make it AKUTAPI, or to 
Russia which would make it RAKUTAPI. I am glad to say that when I made 
this proposal to His Excellency, the President of Pakistan, his response was, "It 
sounded a very good proposal because the vowels and the consonants fall into 
place". 
So, we are imaginatively attempting to tackle this question, and I do 
believe that the vast gas resources of Ce ntral Asia should not be limited to an 
extent that it may not be available in Turkmenistan. And, it remains a very 
important future source of gas for us. 
As regards the pipeline that is coming from Iran, I am glad to inform the hon. 
Member that we had a very constructive meeting of the Joint Working Group 
between India and Pakistan on that pipeline, and each one of these issues that she 
raised has been flagged by us, and we will be considering this further in the next 
meeting of the JWG which is scheduled in the last week of August in Islamabad. 
With Iran, we have held a series of discussions with them over the last seven or 
eight months, and this is now getting formalised into what is called a Special 
Joint Working Group on the pipeline between India and Iran. Their meeting is 
scheduled to begin tomorrow, and we will be addressing some of these questions. 
Now the initial negotiating position of Iran is to base the cost, on which they will 
supply the gas to us, at the opportunity cost, that is, at a cost comparable to the 
kind of prices which can be realised from other markets. And we have taken the 
position that it has to be at a price that is affordable to us primarily in terms of the 
kinds of prices we may hope to be able to charge for the electricity and fertiliser 
that would be produced from that gas, and we have explained the rationale of this 
to them. I have told the Iranians, and they are considering it, that whereas the unit 
price of gas supplied to India might well have to be considerably lower than the 
unit price at which they make LNG supplies to other countries, if they take the 
total quantity of gas that could come to Pakistan and India through that 
pipeline, and the period for which it is guaranteed, which is the life-term of that 
pipeline, then, the total revenues earned by Iran from the gas could be much 
higher. So, these are matters which are seriously under consideration, and I shall 
continue to keep the House and the hon. Member informed of the progress.

having given me the background about the two projects which I thought have 
already been shared. My main question was this. How is the pricing going to be 
compatible with LNG? Keeping that in ivew,4 would now further ask of the hon. 
Minister: Putting aside the pricing and costing which the explained, there is 
another factor in this; that is, you want guarantees from Pakistan for the safe 
transit through Baluchistan. You have no doubt talked of costs, meetings of 
August-September, round-table meetings, etc. But, as you have yourself 
mentioned in your reply to the House, this is a regional thing when we are 
talking of Turkmenistan. Whatever I have read on this subject, I am told that the 
gas which Iran is planning to pipe and send to India is also a regional affair, and

you are going to mobilise resources? What is going to be the end pricing? Is it 
going to be compatible with LNG? And, are you going to get sufficient gas or is

SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR. I think the hon. Member means 
'competitive', not 'compatible'. Taking that to be the meaning of her question, I would 
like to assure her that we are in a very deep commercial relationship on LNG with 
Qatar, and that, when his Highness, the Ameer of Qatar had come to India in 
April, we discussed with him the possibility of our being able to meet at least 
20 million tonnes of our LNG requirements from Qatar in a kind of ten-year 
period from now. My Secretary was in Qatar only yesterday. He is on his way 
back just now, discussing these matters further. We have raised with Qatar the 
possibility of our becoming a part of what is called the GUSA pipeline, which is, 
the Gulf to South Asia pipeline, in which Pakistan is already a member. 
And they informed me, when I was in Islamabad, that they would have no 
objection to India becoming a member. We have taken it up with Qatar and Qatar 
has pointed out to various difficulties that there are in actually realising that 
project. But the fact of the matter is that it is not only Qatar from where we are 
looking for LNG; if it does not work out by pipeline through Bangladesh, we 
might also make it from Myanmar to India. We are also in negotiation with a 
whole sheaf of other countries which include Malaysia, Indonesia, Australia and 
so on. We are taking about what could be obtained, perhaps, from Oman. There is 
some talk of actually investing 
23 

 
RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2005] 
in a gasification plant in Saudi Arabia and so on and so forth. So, whatever we 
might get by pipeline from either Myanmar or Turkmenistan or Iran would 
complement whatever else we are able to obtain by way of LNG. The problem 
with LNG, at least, for the next decade or so, is going to be that there is a 
tremendous shortage or cryogenic ships. It also takes a long time to build, on 
the one hand, a gasification plant in the suppling country and, on the other, 
atermial and re-gasification plant in  the receiving country. There are 
technological innovations taking place such as the one in which a Belgian 
company which has got re-gasification facilities on the ship itself so that you do 
not need a terminal at the other end; from a single mooring you may be able to 
take the pipeline on land. So, all these developments are taking place. We are 
conscious of all of them and we are trying to optimise the basket by which we 
will be able to meet our humungous energy requirements. In any case, whatever 
we get by pipeline would be most useful for western, northern and eastern India. I 
think in peninsular India, at least, for a long time to come, until we work out 
the technological problems of deep-sea piping, it will have to be done by LNG. 
With regard to pricing, we have stressed to the Iranians, and we are going to 
do this with everybody else, that it is only if the prices are affordable india, in 
terms of the fact that power and fertiliser units are the main consumers of gas, 
that we would be ready to enter into a deal with them. So negotiations are on 
and it is not surprising that we have the initial position of the seller asking for 
the higher possible price and, we, the buyers, asking for the least possible 
price. That is how negotiations are conducted, whether in a saree shop or in 
respect to pipelines.

hardening of international prices of crude oil. The average Brent crude oil prices,

project of the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas for radically revamping 
the PDS kerosene distribution network with the primary objective of ensuring that 
this heavily subsidized project is actually made available in the required quantities

and eventually eliminate the diversion of PDS SKO for adulteration. The pilot

transportation of PDS kerosene to ensure widespread public 
information and transparency as these TTs will prominently display the 
special logo that is being devised for the dedicated fleet. It will be clearly 
written on the outside of the TT that it is transporting kerosene meant

special logo, for the delivery of SKO to sub-wholesale points on or 
more barrel sheds;

supervision and respons ibility of the OMCs, who will provide an 
adequate number of barrels, decorated with the special logo, at the 
sub-wholesale point for the convenient and assured transportation of 
PDS SKO to the retails points. Similar logos will be displayed on 
vehicles transporting PDS SKO from wholesale to sub-wholesale 
points and from there to retail points at Fair Price Shops;

progress was reached on Parechu issue.

take measures for controlled release of accumulated water of the landside dam

SHRIMATI JAMANA DEVI BARUPAL:

(a) whether the Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers on 
85 

RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2005] 
VAT has given fresh sweeteners to ensure easy implementation of VAT and 
also achieve convergence in VAT rates; 
(b) if so, whether in the meeting held on April 2005, the Committee 
exempted certain items of mass consumptions like salts and breads of all kind 
(branded and unbranded) and also these items under the PDS; 
(c) the main items exempted from VAT and to what extent this decision has 
been helpful to the consumers as well as traders; and 
(d) whether Committee has also agreed to  reconsider further exemption of

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) to (c) The Empowered Committee of State 
Finance Ministers decided to revise the rates of VAT in respect of certain 
commodities in its meeting held on 26 April 2005, after due consideration of the

general review of rates of VAT at this stage.

powers to empower Panchayati Raj Institutions, including Gram Panchayats, 
to function as "institutions,.of self-Government" for the twin purpose of (i)

Ministers of Panchayati Raj to ensure that on the basis of Activity Mapping, 
Panchayats at various levels are devolved with funds, functions and 
functionaries to enable them to emerge as institutions of self-Government. Efforts

go that Gram Panchayats are made responsible to the Village Community as a 
whole.

Chairmanship of the Secretary (Panchayati Raj) to monitor the progress on the

CNG stations in Tamil Nadu 
897. SHRI R. S HUNMUGASUNDARAM: Will the Minister of 
PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of CNG filling stations which have been established in Tamil Nadu for 
the use of automobiles and what are the places at which, they are functioning; 
(b) whether there is any proposal to increase the number of retail selling CNG 
stations; and 
(c) if so, the places at which they are likely to be established in Tamil Nadu? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) At present, there are no CNG filling stations in Tamil Nadu. 
(b) and (c) CNG will be progressively introduced in polluted cities, including those 
in Tamil Nadu, with the expansion of the pipeline infrastructure and the increased 
availability of natural gas, and also subject to economic viability. 
Promotion of LPG as auto fuel 
898. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether It is a fact that many cities have been affected dye to high vehicular 
pollution in the country; 
(b) if so, what is the Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) whether Government are considering to encourage use of CNG or LPG as a fuel for 
controlling the vehicular pollution in the country; if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether Government are aware that a large number of vehicles are running on LPG 
without proper permission in the-country; and 
(e) if so, what are Government's views and the reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (c) Use of CNG and auto LPG is being encouraged to 
reduce pollution in various cities. Subject to availability of natural gas and necessary 
infrastructure, CNG is proposed to be 
134 

[2 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA  
introduced in various cities in a phased manner. Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) are also 
progressively introducing auto LPG at their retail outlets in different cities as per the 
demand. 
As on July, 2005, the State-wise details of CNG stations of JVs/PSUs are as under:— 
 
State City No. of CNG stations 
Delhi Delhi  133 
Uttar Pradesh Noida  2 
Maharasthra Mumbai  106 
Gujarat Vadodara & Vaghodia 02*

*A few CNG outlets have also been set up by some private/multi-national companies in Gujarat. 
As on 1.4.2005,105 Auto LPG Dispensing Stations (ALDS) are also in operation in 
the country. 
(d) and (e) Yes, Sir. The following measures have been taken by the Government to 
forestall the misuse of domestic LPG cylinders in vehicles:— 
(i) State Governments have been advised to impress upon district authorities the 
need to intensify their supervision of LPG driven vehicles and take action as 
per law in case of violations. 
(ii) Supplies to domestic LPG distributors are regulated by the Oil Marketing 
Companies (OMCs) in line with the customer population and per capita 
consumption of that market, based on last year's sales for the same month. 
(iii) Publicity campaigns are launched by OMCs from time to time to make the 
public aware about the hazards associated with the unauthorized use of 
domestic LPG cylinders as auto LPG.

diesel and other petroleum products to European and other countries where

as the demand in our neighbouring countries as also in the middle-east, China, 
Africa, etc. is rising?

SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) India is already a net exporter of petroleum products. Further, in view

feasibility study on making India as an investment destination for refineries, in 
particular export-oriented refineries, with the main aim of exporting petroleum 
products. We are also attempting through diplomatic channels and meetings of 
Ministers to ascertain whether Indian refining companies could set up a production 
base in the European Union, for example, Romania which is expected to join the 
European Union by January, 2007.

operators and travel agents do not blur the image of India with foreign 
tourists? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF TOURISM (SHRIMATI 
RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Guidelines relating to approval of travel agents and tour operators are 
given in the Statement (See below). 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2005] 
(c) A Complaint Cell has been set up in the Ministry of Tourism to redress 
complaints from tourists. On receipt of specific complaints against tour operators 
and travel agents, the matter is investigated and appropriate action taken 
based on the findings. 
Statement 
Guidelines for recognition as approved Travel Agents & Tour Operators 
The following conditions must be fulfilled by the Travel Agency for grant of 
recognition by Ministry of Tourism: 
(i) The application for grant of recognition shall be in the prescribed form and 
submitted in duplicate with a non-refundable fee of Rs. 3000/- 
(ii) The Travel Agency has a minimu m paid-up capital (or capital employed) 
of Rs. 3.00 lakhs duly supported by the audited balance sheet/Chartered 
Accountant's Certificate. 
(iii) The Travel Agency should be approved by International Air Transport 
Association (IATA) or should be General Sales Agent (GSA)/ 
Passenger Sales Agent (PSA) of an IATA member Airlines. 
(iv) The Travel Agency should have been in operation for a minimum period 
of one year before the date of application. 
(v) The minimum office space should be 250 sq. ft. besides, the office may be 
located in a neat and clean surrounding and equipped with telephone, fax 
and computer reservation system etc. There should be sufficient space for 
reception and easy access to toilet facilities. 
(vi) The Travel Agency should be under the charge of a full time member who is 
adeouately trained, experienced in matters regarding ticketing, itineraries, 
transport, accommodation facilities, currency, customs regulations and 
travel and tourism related services. Besides this, greater emphasis may be 
given to effective communication skills, knowledge of foreign languages, 
other than English. There should be minimum of four qualified staff out 
of which at least two should have Diploma/Degree in Travel and 
Tourism from recognised University, IITTM or Institutions approved by 
AICTE. 
164 

[2 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
The academic qualifications may be relaxed in case of exceptionally 
experienced personnel in Airlines, Shipping, Transport and PR 
agencies, Hotel and other Corporate Bodies and those who have worked 
for 3 years with IATA/UFTA Agencies. 
The academic qualifications may also be relaxed in cases where the travel 
agency companies are located at North-east, religious, remote and small 
cities. There should be a minimum of two qualified staff. 
(vii) The Travel Agency is an income-tax assessee and has filed Income Tax 
Return for the current assessment year. 
(viii) The Travel Agency should empl oyee only Regional guides trained and 
licensed by the Department of Tourism, Government of India and State Level 
guides as well as local guides approved by State Governments. 
(ix) For outsourcing any of the services relating to tourists, the travel agencies 
shall use approved specialised agencies in the specific field of activity. 
The Tour Operator must fulfill the following conditions for grant of 
recognition: 
(i) The application for grant of recognition shall be in the prescribed form 
and submitted in duplicate with a non-refundable fee of Rs. 3000/-. 
(ii) The Tour operator should have a minimum paid-up capital (or capital 
employed) of Rs. 3.00 lakhs duly supported by the latest audited 
balance sheet/Chartered Accountant's Certificate. 
(iii) The turn-over in terms of foreign exchange by the firm from tour 
operation only should be a minimum of Rs. 10.00 lakhs duly supported 
by-Chartered Accountant's Certificate. 
(iv) The Tour Operator has an office under the charge of a full time member of their 
staff, who is adequately trained/experienced in matters regarding 
transport, accommodation, currency, customs regulatios and general 
information about travel and tourism related services. However, greater 
emphasis may be given to effective communication skills and knowledge of 
foreign language other than English. 
165 

RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2005] 
(v) There should be a minimum of four qualified staff out of which at least 
two should have Diploma/Degree in Travel and Tourism from recognised 
University, IITTM or an institution approved by AICTE. 
(vi) The academic qualifications may be relaxed in case of experienced 
personnel in Airlines, Shipping, Transport, PR Agencies, Hotels and other 
corporate bodies and those who have 2 years experience with Department 
of Tourism approved tour operators. 
(vii) Similarly, for the ag encies located at North-east, religious, remote and 
small cities, there should be a minimum of two qualified staff. 
(viii) The Tour Operator should have been in Operation for a minimum 
period of one year before the date of application. 
(ix) The minimum office space should be of 250 sq. ft. besides the office may 
be located in neat and clean surroundings and equipped with telephone, 
fax and computer reservation system etc. There should be sufficient space 
for reception and easy access to toilets. 
(x) The Tour Operator should be an income tax assessee and should have 
filed Income Tax Returns for the last or current assessment year. 
(xi) Tour Operator should employ only Regional Guides trained and licensed 
by the Department of Tourism, Government of India and State level 
Guides approved by the State Governments. 
(xii) The Tour Operator shall contract/use approved specialised agencies in the 
field of adventure options and related services for the tourists.

foreign tourists visited India generating Rs. 21,828 crores in foreign exchange,

exchange of Rs. 72,600 crores, thereby neutralising the foreign exchange 
earnings from tourism, as the Indian tourist, reportedly, finds visiting

resorts; and

tourists arrived in India during 2004, and foreign exchange earnings were Rs. 
21,828 crore. During the year, 6.2 million Indians went abroad and Travel 
payments, as compiled by the Reserve Bank of India, were Rs. 22,988 crore. 
There are various reasons for more Indians going abroad, like fascination for 
foreign locations; prestige involved in visiting foreign c ountries; visiting 
friends and relatives settled in countri es like UK, USA, Singapore, Bahrain, 
Oman, UAE, etc.; cheap/concessional air fares to some foreign locations like

Introduction of roof top Water Harvesting

(a) whether there is any plan to introduce Roof Top Water Harvesting in the 
country;

RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2005]  
(b) if so, the names of States where this system has been introduced; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAI PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
'Water' being a State subject, it is primarily the responsibility of the concerned State 
Governments to make plans for introduction of roof top rain water harvesting in their 
respective States. However, during the Ninth Five Year Plan", the Central Ground 
Water Board (CGWB), under the Ministry of Water Resources, have implemented 
successfully the Central Sector Scheme of 'Study of Recharge to Ground Water' 
under which 67 schemes of roof top rain water harvesting in the States of 
Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Delhi, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu & 
Kashmir, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Mizoram, 
Nagaland, Orissa, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal 
and Union Territories of Lakshadweep and Chandigarh were implemented. The 
CGWB has also organised mass awareness and training programmes for 
promoting roof top rain water narvestina. Demonstrative projects of roof top 
rain water harvesting were also implemented through Community Based 
Organisations/Voluntary Organisations/Voluntary Agencies in rural Government 
schools in the States of Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Himachal 
Pradesh, Jharkhand, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Manipur, Meghalaya, 
Nagaland, Orissa, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, Uttaranchal and West 
Bengal. 
The States of Goa, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Karnataka, 
Kerala, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, 
West Bengal and Union Territories of Daman & Diu, Lakshadweep, NCT of Delhi and 
Pondicherry have also taken steps to introduce rooftop rain water harvesting in their 
respective States/ Union Territories.

Sir, the Government is continuously monitoring the price situation. The  
pricing   mechanism  attempts  to  balance  the  interests  of various stakeholders, 
viz., consumers, Government and oil companies. 
With a view to containing the burden of the increase in international prices on the 
prices of sensitive petroleum products, it has been decided to maintain the price of domestic 
LPG and PDS kerosene, notwithstanding, the steep rise in international prices of these 
products but to allow for a moderate increase in domestic retail prices of diesel and 
petrol, so that the burden is equitably shared between Government, oil companies and 
to some extent, by consumers. In this light, the Government reduced the excise duty 
on petrol and diesel by four per cent and three per cent respectively effective 16.06.2004, 
and effective 19.08.2004, the excise duty on petrol and diesel was further reduced by three 
per cent. The Government also reduced customs duty by five per cent each on petrol and 
diesel with effect from 19.08.2004. In the Budget 2005-06, a reduction in customs duty on 
crude from ten per cent to five per cent and in other petroleum products from the range of 
15-20 per cent to 10 per cent was announced.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI S. 
REGUPATHY): There were unprecedented rains in Konkan and other parts of 
Maharashtra causing extensive flooding in many parts of the , State. From 22nd July 
onwards, the rainfall had been more than 100 mm on an average per day in all the 
districts. On July 26th, the suburban areas of Mumbai and Thane districts received record 
rainfall. Between 26th and 27th July, 2005, that is, within a span of 24 hours, Mumbai and 
suburban areas recorded unprecedented rainfall of 920 mm, a phenomenon which had 
never occurred before. Thane district also received more than 700 mm rains in a single 
day. In Thane district, all the urban centres were severely flooded. Kalyan, Dombivali, 
Ambarnath, Ulhasnagar and Bhiwandi, which are part of the urban agglomeration, 
were under flood waters. 
The rains had slowed down after July 28, 2005, but since last two days, it 
has been raining heavily and rainfall, as on July 31, 2005 and August 1, 2005, at 8.30 
hrs. in the morning, in last 24 hrs., was 63.6 mms and 89.8 mms at Colaba and 161 
mms and 208.10 mms at Santacruz, respectively. 
In the Konkan region, Raigad ana Ratnagiri districts recorded heavy rains 
and large areas were submerged. The towns, which were severely affected by 
floods, are Roha, Mahad and Mangaon in Raigad district, and Kher and Chiplun in 
Ratnagiri districts. This heavy rainfall triggered landslides affecting six villages in 
Raigad and Ratnagiri. In village Jui, near Mahad in Raigad district, about 100 people 
are feared dead due to collapse of houses. 
In Marathwada, Parbhani and Nanded districts experienced severe flooding.   
In Parbhani, due to the rise of river Dudhna, a number of villages 
262 

[2 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
were marooned, while in Nanded district, the rise in the water level in river  
Godavari affected more than 100 villages. 
Due to these spells of heavy and unprecedented rains, 17 out of 35 districts 
in Maharashtra have been affected. The number of villages reported to be 
affected are 300. 929 persons are reported to have lost their lives, 72 persons have 
suffered injuries, while 100 persons are reported missing. The flood impacted the life 
of approximately 1.20 crore people and more than 50,000 persons were evacuated 
to safer places. A large number of livestock perished in Mumbai and other cities. In 
Mumbai alone, 1,200 buffalos and 15,000 sheep and goats perished in the floods. 
The heavy rains and floods caused extensive damage to infrastructure and 
communication.   Most of the roads in suburban Mumbai had at least 3 to 4 feet of 
water flowing over them paralysing traffic movement in Mumbai. A large number of 
office employees, school children and public were stranded and had difficulty 
in accessing their homes. 
The Mumbai-Goa National Highway was cut off at many points due to large 
tracks being submerged. The traffic on this highway was completely disrupted. The 
Mumbai-Pune expressway was also affected. 
The Western and' Central Railway had to stop their local trains. The Konkan 
railway was also submerged at many places, as a result of which a number of trains 
were stranded at various destinations. Air services were also adversely affected due 
to heavy rains and poor visibility. 
There was damage to other public infrastructure viz. public buildings, water 
supply schemes, primary health centres. The telecommunication network was also 
badly disrupted. Water and power supply system were affected in many areas. 
The State Government has initiated relief measures on a warfooting to restore 
normalcy in the city of Mumbai and other places in the State. The State Government 
has started disbursement of foodgrains and kerosene; 10 Kgs of rice, 10 Kgs of wheat 
and 10 Litres of kerosene is being disbursed to each affected family. The State 
Government has also started distributing ex gratia assistance to all families @ Rs. 
1000/- per person, subject to a maximum of Rs.5,ooo/- per family. Heirs of deceased 
will be given cash assistance of Rs.2 lakh (Rs.1 lakh from PM's Relief Fund and Rs.1 
lakh from the  State  Government).    So far, ex gratia 'assistance  of Rs.10 
crore 
263 

RAJYA SABHA [2 A ugust, 2005] 
{approximately) has been disbursed to the affected families.   (As on August 1, 2005 
morning) 
Monitoring teams have been appointed under the Chairmanship of Guardian 
Secretaries of the Districts. Similarly, a State level team of Secretary level officers 
has also been set up to coordinate and- monitor relief and rescue operations. The 
Guardian Ministers are already in the district headquarters, who are personally 
supervising and guiding the relief and rescue operations. 
In spite of heavy rains, the flood situation has improved considerably in the 
State. Floodwaters have receded in Mumbai, Thane and other areas of Konkan. Due 
to heavy rains in catchment area, surplus water is being released from Koyna, Dhon, 
Veer, Kaner and other reservoirs, which is likely to cause inundation in the downstream 
districts of Sangli, Kolhapur, Solapur, other parts of Western Maharashtra and 
Marathwada. We have requested Armed Forces to stand by for immediate 
deployment should the need arise. So far, six columns of Army have been deployed 
at different places along with six boats. In addition, 8 teams of divers have also 
been deployed. More than 2,000 persons have been evacuated further making a 
total of 52,000 and taken to safer places. 
Top most priority has been given to removal of garbage and providing 
drinking water. The garbage in Thane municipal area has been lifted to a large 
extent by employing 4,000 people, 30 JCBs and 70 dumpers. Nearly eighty per 
cent garbage has been lifted in Panvel. Scavenging work is likely to be completed in 
Mumbai and Navi Mumbai Municipal Corporation areas. It is slow in Kalyan, but 
additional machinery .and personnel has been deployed in scavenging 
operations. The scavenging work is slow in Badlapur.Ambernath, Bhiwandi and other 
areas due to higher water level. It is expected that all these small cities would be able 
to finish the garbage disposal in next two days. 
Full water supply has been restored in Thane, Mira-Bhayander, Navi Mumbai, 
Roha, Mahad and Panvel. It has been restored partially in Kalyan, Dombivili and likely 
to be normal by today evening. The normal water supply in Ambemath and 
Badlapur is 70 mid; so far as 24 mid supply has been restored, rest will be restored 
in next two days. The water supply in Mumbai has been restored in about 90 per 
cent area. Drinking water is being provided through tankers, where it has not been 
possible to restore, water supply.   More than 300 tankers have been deployed for this 
purpose. 
264 

[2 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Electricity has been restored in all the areas except in some parts of 
Mumbai, where the supply is through Reliance Energy. It will be restored 
everywhere by today evening. All possi ble assistance is being provided to 
Reliance Energy by the Maharashtra State Electricity Board to restore power 
supply. 
State Government is paying adequat e attention to health needs of 
people in flood-affected areas. Some cases of diarrhoea have been reported. 
More than 100 teams, consisting of doctors and other medical personnel, have 
been deployed at main railway stations  in Mumbai. They are treating the 
needy patients as well as doing awareness work, for which pamphlets have 
been prepared. Similarly, more than 500 medical units have been deployed in 
remaining 16 flood-affected districts. All essential medicines like chlorine 
tablets, ORS packets, etc. have been made available in adequate quantity. 
The State Government is workin g on warfooting and making all 
possible efforts to provide an early relief to the flood-affected persons. 
The Central Government is providing all required support to the 
Government of Maharashtra to enable them to bring normalcy in the affected 
areas. Honourable Prime Minister, hon. Agriculture Minister and the hon. 
Home Minister had visited the affected areas. They had discussions about the 
situation with the Chief Minister, St ate Officers, Military Officers and the 
representatives of the people. They su rveyed the damage done and flew over 
the areas affected by the heavy rains. The Cabinet Secretary has been 
holding meetings at Delhi to find out the ways and means which can be used 
to help the people in the area. The Government of India has announced the 
ad hoc assistance of Rs. 500 crore, to start with, and the foodgrains. The 
Prime Minister has announced that all other help needed, be given to the 
people and the State. Steps are being ta ken to see that insurance companies 
gear up to help the people. The losses sustained by the people and the State 
would be calculated, and assistance would be given to bring life in the State to 
normalcy. The State Government makes the plan to recoup the losses. The 
same may be discussed with the Planning Commission and other Ministries 
and steps may be taken to restore electricity, water supply, repair of roads 
and construction of houses for the people. 
At this stage, relief and assistance is given. In the second phase, within 
days, temporary arrangement would be made to help the affected 
265 

RAJYA SABHA [2 A ugust, 2005] 
people to resume their normal activities and life. In the third and final phase, the 
infrastructure damaged would be repaired and at places newly built; and the people 
would be helped to carry on with their activities. We would like to hear suggestions 
from the hon. Members for appropriate action.  Thank you.

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
New framework for U.S. - India defence relationship 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): Mr. 
Deputy Chairman, Sir, with your permission, I would like to make a statement 
on U.S.    India Defence Relationship. 
Sir, I made an official visit to  the United States of America 
(USA)recently at the end of June 2005 at  the invitation of the US Secretary of 
Defence. The visit provided an opportunity for an exchange of views with the 
US leadership on international security issues and to promote cooperation with 
the US to strengthen and modernise  our armed forces and our defence 
industries through increased professional interaction in the military sphere and 
collaboration in the sphere of defence equipment and technology in the mutual 
interest of both countries. A document entitled 'New Framework for the US-
India Defence Relationship' was signed during the visit. The 'Framework' 
contains only enabling provisions. It does not contain any commitments or 
obligations. 
The 'Framework' updates the 'Agreed Minutes on Defence Relations 
between India and the United States' signed in January 1995. It identifies 
global security threats that have seriously affected our security, such as 
terrorism and violent religious extremism,  and the proliferat ion of Weapons of 
Mass Destruction (WMD) and related ma terials, data and technologies as 
areas of shared concern, and provides for cooperation with the US to enhance 
our capabilities in responding to t hese and prospects of cooperation in 
advanced and sensitive technologies  and other challenges like natural 
disasters. It reflects our interest in t he security of the sea-lanes and regional 
and global security and stability. It establishes a new Defence Procurement 
and Production Group under the existing  Defence Policy Group to promote a 
defence trade, production and technology relationship with the United States. It 
also provides for a dialogue on international security issues, 
272 

[2 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
and cooperation with the international community to promote regional and global 
stability through cooperative actions in the mutual interest. 
The visit builds on ongoing efforts to expand cooperation with the US in the 
field of high technology by opening up the US as a potential source of advanced 
defence equipment and technology, increasing our options and leverage vis-a-vis 
suppliers in the acquisition of defence technology, promoting cooperation with the 
US to enhance the capabilities of India's Armed forces and defence industries and 
increasing our strategic manoeuvrability in international affairs. 
The 'Framework' document should be seen in this context. Concerns 
expressed in Parliament and in the pr ess on the implications of the document 
have included apprehensions that it commits India to deploying troops in supDort of 
US-led coalition operations in Ireq and possibly elsewhere; that it adopts 
vocabulary and language, and therefore the world view, of the United States; and that 
it. promotes US security interests and not ours, and therefore compromises our 
security. None of these apprehensions are justified. The document, more than 
anything else, signals US wil'ingness to enhance defence cooperation with India and 
strengthen our defence capabilities. It is in our interest to see how we can exploit this 
change of attitude to our advantage, it is an enabling document that provides a 
framework within which specific cooperation can take place. It is up to us how we 
develop this. This will not be dictated to us. It will be decided by mutual 
agreement 
The presumption that "shared" interests involving the US must necessarily 
mean primacy to US interests, reflects a lack of self-confidence in ourselves. As a 
trustee of the legacy of independence, secularism, non-alignment and autonomy and 
independence on our domestic and foreign policies, we have the self-confidence that 
we will be able to recognise and resist anything that is not in our national interest, not 
confuse US interests with ours, or subordinate our interests to US interests.
